steps.action:
# How Transformer Neural Networks Work

## The Core Problem They Solve

Earlier neural networks (RNNs) processed sequences word-by-word, left to right. This made it hard to connect information far apart in a sentence, and it was slow (couldn't parallelize). Transformers solve both problems.

---

## The Big Idea: Attention

Instead of reading sequentially, transformers ask: **"for each word, which other words are most relevant to understanding it?"**

This is the **self-attention mechanism**.

### How Attention Works

For every word (token) in your input, the model creates three vectors:
- **Query (Q)** — "What am I looking for?"
- **Key (K)** — "What do I contain?"
- **Value (V)** — "What do I actually pass along?"

For each token, you compute dot products of its Query against every other token's Key. This produces **attention scores** — how much one token should "attend to" another. Those scores are scaled, softmaxed (turned into probabilities), then used to take a weighted sum of the Values.

Result: each token gets a new representation that's a **blend of all other tokens, weighted by relevance**.

Example: In *"The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired"* — attention lets "it" strongly attend to "animal," resolving the reference.

---

## Multi-Head Attention

Instead of doing attention once, transformers do it **multiple times in parallel** with different learned Q/K/V projections (called "heads"). Each head can learn a different type of relationship (syntactic, semantic, coreference, etc.). Results are concatenated and projected back.

---

## The Full Architecture

```
Input tokens
    ↓
Token Embeddings + Positional Encoding
    ↓
[Transformer Block] × N
    ├── Multi-Head Self-Attention
    ├── Add & Normalize (residual connection)
    ├── Feed-Forward Network (per token, independently)
    └── Add & Normalize
    ↓
Output
```

### Key components:

**Positional Encoding** — Since attention has no inherent sense of order, position information is injected (added to embeddings) so the model knows token 1 comes before token 2.

**Feed-Forward Layer** — After attention mixes information across tokens, a simple MLP processes each token *independently*, adding representational capacity.

**Residual Connections** — Each sublayer's input is added to its output (`x + sublayer(x)`). This helps gradients flow during training and lets layers learn *adjustments* rather than full transformations.

**Layer Normalization** — Stabilizes training by normalizing activations.

---

## Encoder vs. Decoder

**Encoder-only** (e.g., BERT): reads the full input bidirectionally. Good for classification, understanding tasks.

**Decoder-only** (e.g., GPT): generates tokens one at a time, can only attend to *past* tokens (causal masking). Good for generation.

**Encoder-Decoder** (e.g., original Transformer, T5): encoder reads input, decoder generates output attending to both past outputs and encoder representations. Good for translation, summarization.

---

## Why Transformers Work So Well

| Property | Benefit |
|---|---|
| Full sequence attention | Captures long-range dependencies |
| Parallelizable | Trains efficiently on GPUs |
| Scalable | Performance keeps improving with more data/parameters |
| General | Same architecture works for text, images, audio, code |

---

## The Training Loop (briefly)

- Feed in text, predict the next token (or masked tokens)
- Compare prediction to reality (cross-entropy loss)
- Backpropagate, adjust weights
- Do this billions of times

The model learns *what to attend to* and *how to transform representations* entirely from data.

---

## One-Line Summary

> A transformer learns to build rich representations of each token by repeatedly asking "which other tokens matter for understanding this one?" and blending their information — all at once, in parallel, across many learned relationship types.
